The Fatimid Caliphate. From 909 to 1171 of the common era, this was a Shiite dynasty centered in North Africa and later Egypt, which claimed descent from Fatima, the daughter of Muhammad, and challenged the Sunni Abbasid caliphate's legitimacy for over 250 years. At their height, the Fatimids controlled Egypt, Sicily, and the Mediterranean trade routes, becoming one of the medieval world's wealthiest powers before being overtaken by the Ayyubid dynasty.

The dynasty was named after Fatima, Muhammad's daughter, and they claimed her line carried divine right to rule—a fundamental Shiite doctrine that delegitimized Sunni leadership. They rose in Tunisia under Abdallah al-Mahdi in 909, spreading westward through North Africa before conquering Egypt in 969 and establishing Cairo as their capital. In Cairo they founded Al-Azhar University, one of Islam's oldest and most prestigious institutions, and it remains a center of Islamic learning to this day. The Fatimids controlled the Red Sea and Mediterranean trade routes, accumulating vast wealth from spice, silk, and strategic commerce, transforming Cairo into a glittering cosmopolitan center. They practiced remarkable religious tolerance toward Christians, Jews, and other minorities within their realm, fostering a pluralistic urban culture distinct from their Sunni neighbors. But they weakened under Crusader invasions in the Levant and internal administrative decay. Finally they fell to Saladin's Ayyubid dynasty in 1171, which restored Sunni orthodoxy to Egypt.

The Abbasid Caliphate was the rival power they challenged for theological and political supremacy. The Ayyubid dynasty conquered Egypt from them. Al-Azhar University endured from their founding. And their period coincided with the Crusades, which inflicted military conflict on their Levantine territories.
